title: How to Choose Real-World Objects for Your TOK…
summary: Learn how to choose three specific real-world TOK exhibition objects, test their prompt links, avoid generic examples, and plan effectively this fall.
body_markdown:
To choose real-world objects for a TOK exhibition, begin with one official IA prompt and identify three **specific, traceable objects** that reveal different answers, tensions, or perspectives. A strong object is not merely related to the topic. Its origin, use, audience, or history must help you analyze how knowledge is produced, justified, interpreted, communicated, or challenged.


This process is particularly useful during the **IB TOK fall term** , when many students move from prompt selection to object research. Test several possibilities before committing so that you have time to verify each object’s context, obtain an appropriate image, and develop three distinct arguments.


### Understand the official TOK exhibition requirements


The[IB overview of Theory of Knowledge](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/theory-of-knowledge/what-is-tok/) explains that the exhibition explores how TOK manifests in the world around us. According to the[official TOK subject brief](https://ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/tok-sb-english.pdf) , it is internally assessed, externally moderated, and contributes **one-third** of the TOK result.


Your submitted exhibition must include:


- **One official IA prompt** , reproduced exactly
- **Three objects** , or images of objects, linked to that prompt
- An image and clear identification of each object
- The **specific real-world context** of each object
- An explanation of its link to the prompt
- A justification of its particular contribution
- Appropriate citations and references
- No more than **950 words** across the commentaries


Objects may be physical or digital. A particular social media post, online map, data visualization, photograph, or archived webpage can qualify when it has a specific context. Student-created objects can also work if they already existed and were not manufactured solely for the assessment.


The IB recommends connecting the exhibition to a TOK theme, but the central assessed task is to establish and justify each object’s relationship with the selected prompt. A personal connection may make this easier, but personal significance is not a formal requirement.


### What makes an object specific and real-world?


A specific object is an identifiable instance rather than a general category. It normally has contextual details such as a creator, date, location, owner, audience, publication, function, or documented history.


Too generic Specific real-world object


A newspaper The front page of a named newspaper published after a particular election


A medical test A laboratory report issued to a patient on a known date


A map The evacuation map displayed in your school science building


A social media post A dated post from an identifiable account responding to a specific event


A family photograph A photograph taken by your grandmother during a documented migration


Specificity matters because TOK analysis depends on context. A generic map may symbolize knowledge, but a school evacuation map lets you examine who produced it, what information was selected, why users trust it, and how practical purposes shape knowledge.


Complete this sentence before selecting an object: **“This is the particular object created or used by ___ at ___ in ___ for the purpose of ___.”** If you cannot fill in the gaps, the object may be too vague or poorly researched.


### Work from the prompt, not the object


A common mistake is choosing three interesting objects and then searching for a prompt that loosely accommodates them. Instead, read the official prompt exactly and identify its decisive words. In “What counts as good evidence for a claim?”, for example, the key ideas include **counts** , **good evidence** , and **claim** .


Use those words to ask:


- Who decides what counts as evidence here?
- By what standards is it judged?
- Do those standards change between communities?
- What limitation does the object expose?
- What happens when the evidence is accepted or rejected?


The[RevisionDojo guide to TOK exhibition prompts](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-exhibition-prompts) can help you unpack the wording. Your final exhibition must reproduce the selected prompt exactly, even if you paraphrase it privately while planning.


### Give the three objects different jobs


Your objects should not produce three versions of the same argument. A coherent exhibition often gives each one a distinct analytical role.


Object role Purpose


Initial case Establishes a plausible answer to the prompt


Complication Introduces uncertainty, bias, disagreement, or limitation


Perspective shift Examines another community, method, culture, time, or area of knowledge


For the prompt “What role do experts play in influencing our consumption or acquisition of knowledge?”, a specific prescription label might demonstrate reliance on medical expertise. A retracted scientific paper could complicate trust in experts. A family remedy recorded in a relative’s notebook might raise questions about expertise outside formal institutions.


The objects need not be directly connected, but together they must create a purposeful exploration of the same prompt. The[RevisionDojo TOK object ideas guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-exhibition-object-ideas) provides models of specificity, not objects to copy.


### Apply a five-part object test


Evaluate each candidate using five questions:


1. **Specific:** Can I identify the exact object rather than only its category?
2. **Traceable:** Can I verify its creator, origin, use, or date?
3. **Prompt-linked:** Can I explain its relationship to the exact prompt in one defensible sentence?
4. **Analysable:** Does it reveal something about evidence, authority, interpretation, values, certainty, methods, or perspective?
5. **Distinct:** Does it contribute an idea that my other objects do not?


A strong candidate should pass every test. The[RevisionDojo guide to selecting TOK objects](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/selecting-the-right-objects-for-your-tok-exhibition) offers a companion checklist.


Then write about 100 words explaining the object’s context, prompt link, and unique contribution. If most of the paragraph describes its appearance, the object may not generate enough TOK analysis.


### Plan object selection during the fall term


Your school determines its internal schedule, so teacher deadlines take priority. A practical September-November plan is:


### September: explore


Shortlist two or three prompts and generate at least five possible objects for each. Photograph personal or local objects, save publication details for digital materials, and record each candidate’s origin.


### October: test


Choose one prompt and four or five serious candidates. Write a one-sentence knowledge claim for each, then select the three that create the strongest contrast. Confirm that images are clear and contextual claims can be referenced.


### November: draft


Draft approximately **280-320 words per object** , adjusting the balance while remaining within the combined 950-word limit. Check that every commentary identifies context, explains the prompt link, and justifies the object’s distinctive role. Use[annotated TOK exhibition examples](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars/tok-exhibition) to study structure, while preserving your own objects and reasoning.


### Common object-selection mistakes


Avoid selecting an object merely because it is famous, emotional, or easy to photograph. Other common problems include:


- Using a stock image instead of a documented object
- Choosing three objects from nearly identical contexts
- Explaining an event without analyzing the object’s epistemic significance
- Saying an object “relates to knowledge” without addressing the prompt
- Using an object whose context cannot be verified
- Treating personal meaning as a substitute for analysis
- Inventing an object specifically for the assessment


Ask: **“Why is this particular object especially useful for answering this particular prompt?”** The commentary should answer that question explicitly.


### Conclusion


Strong TOK exhibition objects are specific, contextualized, traceable, and capable of supporting different knowledge arguments. Select the prompt first, test more than three candidates, and ensure every chosen object makes a distinct contribution.
